title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
description: A young scientist gives life to a being he then abandons. Rejected by everyone, the creature learns to read, to reason and to hate, and demands from its maker the one thing he refuses: a companion.
source_title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus (1831 edition)

cover.alt: The creature wakes on the floor among bones and books while Victor flees through the door
cover.credit: Theodor von Holst (drawing) and William Chevalier (engraving), for Frankenstein (Colburn and Bentley, 1831). Public domain.

elements.title: A ship in the ice
elements.text: The explorer Robert Walton, trapped in Arctic ice on his way to the Pole, takes aboard a half-frozen stranger who has been chasing a giant figure across the floes.

metadata.source_quote: He was soon borne away by the waves, and lost in darkness and distance.

image.alt: A ship crushed between towering blocks of ice
image.credit: Nipped in the Ice, Currier & Ives, 1877–94. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Lightning and the oak
elements.text: As a boy in Geneva, Victor watches lightning reduce an oak to ribbons, and turns from old alchemy to modern science.

metadata.source_quote: on a sudden I beheld a stream of fire issue from an old and beautiful oak

image.alt: A storm darkening over a lake, a man and a boy waiting on the shore
image.credit: Approaching Thunder Storm, Martin Johnson Heade, 1859. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Departure for Ingolstadt
elements.text: His mother dies of scarlet fever; Victor leaves Elizabeth and his family for the university.

metadata.source_quote: The day of my departure at length arrived.

image.alt: Elizabeth holding Victor's hand at the door as he leaves for Ingolstadt, his face in his hand
image.credit: Theodor von Holst (drawing) and William Chevalier (engraving), for Frankenstein (Colburn and Bentley, 1831). Public domain.

elements.title: The workshop of filthy creation
elements.text: For two years Victor builds a body from the dissecting room and the slaughter-house, in a cell at the top of his lodgings.

metadata.source_quote: I kept my workshop of filthy creation

image.alt: A satirical print of a corpse sitting up in its coffin, jolted by galvanism
image.credit: A Galvanized Corpse, Henry R. Robinson, 1836. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: It breathed
elements.text: On a November night the creature opens its eyes. Victor flees, and the creature wanders out into the world alone.

metadata.source_quote: I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard, and a convulsive motion agitated its limbs.

image.alt: The creature wakes on the floor among bones and books while Victor flees through the door
image.credit: Theodor von Holst (drawing) and William Chevalier (engraving), for Frankenstein (Colburn and Bentley, 1831). Public domain.

elements.title: William and Justine
elements.text: Victor's little brother William is strangled near Geneva. The servant Justine is hanged for it; Victor knows the real killer and stays silent.

image.alt: Lake Geneva with trees and boats in the foreground
image.credit: View of Lake Geneva, Joseph Vernet, ca. 1750–1800. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Meeting on the glacier
elements.text: On the Mer de Glace the creature confronts its maker and asks to be heard.

metadata.source_quote: For some time I sat upon the rock that overlooks the sea of ice.

image.alt: The Mer de Glace glacier below the peaks of Chamonix, in mezzotint
image.credit: Mêr de Glace, Valley of Chamouni-Savoy, Joseph Mallord William Turner, May 23, 1812. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: The cottagers
elements.text: Hidden in a hovel beside the De Lacey family's cottage, the creature learns speech and reading, and is driven away the day he shows himself.

metadata.source_quote: I am malicious because I am miserable.

elements.title: A companion
elements.text: The creature asks for a female companion and promises to leave Europe forever. Victor agrees.

metadata.source_quote: I am alone, and miserable; man will not associate with me

image.alt: The massif of Mont Blanc, its snowy peaks above a stony valley
image.credit: View of the Massif of Mont Blanc, Jean-Antoine Linck, late 18th–19th century. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: The broken promise
elements.text: On a remote Orkney island Victor tears apart the half-finished companion while the creature watches through the window.

metadata.source_quote: You are my creator, but I am your master;--obey!

elements.title: The wedding-night
elements.text: The creature kills Victor's friend Clerval, then Elizabeth on her wedding night. Victor's father dies of grief.

metadata.source_quote: I shall be with you on your wedding-night.

image.alt: A storm darkening over a lake, a man and a boy waiting on the shore
image.credit: Approaching Thunder Storm, Martin Johnson Heade, 1859. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Into the north
elements.text: Victor pursues the creature across Europe and Russia onto the Arctic ice, following the messages it leaves him.

image.alt: A ship among Arctic ice floes under a dark storm cloud
image.credit: An Arctic Summer: Boring Through the Pack in Melville Bay, William Bradford, 1871. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: The creature at the deathbed
elements.text: Victor dies aboard Walton's ship. The creature comes to mourn him, then leaves on an ice raft to die.

image.alt: A ship crushed between towering blocks of ice
image.credit: Nipped in the Ice, Currier & Ives, 1877–94. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Victor Frankenstein
elements.text: A gifted young Genevan who masters the secret of life, then spends the rest of it fleeing the consequences.

metadata.source_quote: Life and death appeared to me ideal bounds, which I should first break through

image.alt: Elizabeth holding Victor's hand at the door as he leaves for Ingolstadt, his face in his hand
image.credit: Theodor von Holst (drawing) and William Chevalier (engraving), for Frankenstein (Colburn and Bentley, 1831). Public domain.

elements.title: The creature
elements.text: Eight feet tall, made from the dead, gentle at first. Self-taught from Milton, Plutarch and Goethe, more eloquent than his maker, and never given a name.

metadata.source_quote: I ought to be thy Adam; but I am rather the fallen angel

image.alt: The creature wakes on the floor among bones and books while Victor flees through the door
image.credit: Theodor von Holst (drawing) and William Chevalier (engraving), for Frankenstein (Colburn and Bentley, 1831). Public domain.

elements.title: Elizabeth Lavenza
elements.text: Victor's adopted sister and later his bride, kind and patient; she pays for his silence.

image.alt: Elizabeth holding Victor's hand at the door as he leaves for Ingolstadt, his face in his hand
image.credit: Theodor von Holst (drawing) and William Chevalier (engraving), for Frankenstein (Colburn and Bentley, 1831). Public domain.

elements.title: Robert Walton
elements.text: An English explorer seeking the North Pole, whose letters to his sister frame the story. Victor's warning is meant for him.

image.alt: A ship among Arctic ice floes under a dark storm cloud
image.credit: An Arctic Summer: Boring Through the Pack in Melville Bay, William Bradford, 1871. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Henry Clerval
elements.text: Victor's cheerful friend, who nurses him through fever and loves poetry and languages.

elements.title: The De Lacey family
elements.text: A blind old man and his children, exiled from France, whom the creature secretly watches and learns from.

elements.title: Geneva and its lake
elements.text: Victor's childhood home at Belrive on Lake Geneva, where storms sweep over the water from the Alps.

image.alt: Lake Geneva with trees and boats in the foreground
image.credit: View of Lake Geneva, Joseph Vernet, ca. 1750–1800. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Ingolstadt
elements.text: The Bavarian university town where Victor studies and builds the creature in an attic laboratory.

elements.title: The Mer de Glace
elements.text: The great glacier below Mont Blanc, where creator and creature meet and argue.

metadata.source_quote: The surface is very uneven, rising like the waves of a troubled sea

image.alt: The Mer de Glace glacier below the peaks of Chamonix, in mezzotint
image.credit: Mêr de Glace, Valley of Chamouni-Savoy, Joseph Mallord William Turner, May 23, 1812. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: The Arctic ice
elements.text: The frozen sea where Walton's ship is trapped and the long chase ends.

image.alt: A ship among Arctic ice floes under a dark storm cloud
image.credit: An Arctic Summer: Boring Through the Pack in Melville Bay, William Bradford, 1871. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Galvanism and natural philosophy
elements.text: The science of the day: electricity that makes dead muscles move, and chemists like Waldman who promise that the moderns have discovered how the blood circulates and command the thunders of heaven.

image.alt: A satirical print of a corpse sitting up in its coffin, jolted by galvanism
image.credit: A Galvanized Corpse, Henry R. Robinson, 1836. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Nested narrators
elements.text: The novel is a story inside a story inside letters: Walton writes down Victor's tale, which contains the creature's own.

image.alt: A ship crushed between towering blocks of ice
image.credit: Nipped in the Ice, Currier & Ives, 1877–94. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: The duty of a maker
elements.text: Victor's real failure is abandonment, not creation. He never asks what he owes the life he made.

image.alt: The creature wakes on the floor among bones and books while Victor flees through the door
image.credit: Theodor von Holst (drawing) and William Chevalier (engraving), for Frankenstein (Colburn and Bentley, 1831). Public domain.

elements.title: Nature or nurture
elements.text: The creature claims he was born good and made bad by how he was treated. The novel lets him make the case without settling it.

metadata.source_quote: I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend.

image.alt: A storm darkening over a lake, a man and a boy waiting on the shore
image.credit: Approaching Thunder Storm, Martin Johnson Heade, 1859. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Dangerous knowledge
elements.text: Victor and Walton are the same ambitious man at different stages; the novel is one warning the other.

metadata.source_quote: how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge

image.alt: Elizabeth holding Victor's hand at the door as he leaves for Ingolstadt, his face in his hand
image.credit: Theodor von Holst (drawing) and William Chevalier (engraving), for Frankenstein (Colburn and Bentley, 1831). Public domain.

elements.title: Loneliness
elements.text: What the creature asks for is not power but company. Its violence starts when it understands it will always be alone.

metadata.source_quote: Every where I see bliss, from which I alone am irrevocably excluded.

image.alt: The massif of Mont Blanc, its snowy peaks above a stony valley
image.credit: View of the Massif of Mont Blanc, Jean-Antoine Linck, late 18th–19th century. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Paradise Lost
elements.text: The creature reads Milton's epic as a true history and compares himself to Adam and to Satan; its lines were the epigraph of the first edition (1818).

elements.title: Prometheus
elements.text: The Titan who made humans from clay and stole fire for them, punished forever: the novel's subtitle.

elements.title: The Villa Diodati, 1816
elements.text: Mary Shelley began the story at a ghost-story contest with Byron, Percy Shelley and John Polidori on Lake Geneva.

image.alt: Lake Geneva with trees and boats in the foreground
image.credit: View of Lake Geneva, Joseph Vernet, ca. 1750–1800. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.

elements.title: Galvani and Aldini
elements.text: Luigi Galvani's twitching frog legs and Giovanni Aldini's public experiments on corpses made reanimation seem almost possible.

image.alt: A satirical print of a corpse sitting up in its coffin, jolted by galvanism
image.credit: A Galvanized Corpse, Henry R. Robinson, 1836. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.
